## Nearest in meaning is not the same as relevant {#jacob-vectors .motion}

```{=html}
<div class="jacob-map"><span class="on">1 Problem</span><span>2 Graphs</span><span>3 Agents</span><span>4 Scale</span></div>
```

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.jacob-list}
Standard retrieval (RAG): chunk the documents, embed them, return the top *k* chunks by cosine similarity.

In my test (1.46 million chunks):

- Averaged **13.0 / 25**, second-lowest of 8 systems
- Customs records rarely ranked highest by similarity, so it **could not answer any quantitative question**
- Long narrative books can outrank the short letters and tables that hold the facts
:::
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{=html}

:::

::: notes
1–2. This audience knows embeddings and cosine similarity, so don't define them. Say it in one breath and move to the evidence.

Numbers from chapter 3: 1.46 million chunks embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B in ChromaDB; RAG-only averaged 13/25 across 30 questions. The thesis explains the failure: structured import records, embedded as text alongside narrative documents, rarely scored highest on cosine similarity, and a long treatise on Jamaica's plants can score closer to a sugar-export question than a planter's letter.

The schematic is not data; say so. It shows the retrieval step: the question lands and lines go to its three nearest neighbours.

[What is NER?]{.def-term}
*Named entity recognition*: a model that tags names of people, places, goods and organisations in text, so they can become nodes in a graph.

- OCR: one NVIDIA 5070 Ti (~24 s per page), or 50,000 documents in under 48 hours on the Digital Research Alliance's Nibi cluster

:::
:::

2–3. The stages appear in order. Each number is measured; say where it ran.

Sources: OCR results and throughput, chapter 1 (olmOCR-2 mean WER 0.075 ± 0.107 on the hand-transcribed gold standard; ~24 s per page on a 5070 Ti; under 48 hours for 50,000 documents on Nibi, including queue time). Entity count, chapter 3. Graph size, chapter 3 (Neo4j; first build).

The last box is green because it is the check: a person reads the sources the system ranks.

```

::: {.columns}

```{=html}
<svg class="motion-map" viewBox="0 0 560 270" role="img" aria-label="Bar chart of strict F1 scores: hmBERT 0.156, spaCy 0.198, GLiNER 0.405, Qwen3-4B base 0.490, Gemini 3 Pro 0.665, EarlyModernNER 0.775">
<text x="0" y="14" style="fill:#9a958a">strict F1 (higher is better)</text>
<g class="rise" data-at="400"><text x="0" y="48">hmBERT</text><rect x="170" y="35" width="56" height="20" fill="#7fa7d6"/><text x="232" y="50">0.156</text></g>
<g class="rise" data-at="800"><text x="0" y="86">spaCy</text><rect x="170" y="73" width="71" height="20" fill="#7fa7d6"/><text x="247" y="88">0.198</text></g>
<g class="rise" data-at="1200"><text x="0" y="124">GLiNER</text><rect x="170" y="111" width="146" height="20" fill="#7fa7d6"/><text x="322" y="126">0.405</text></g>
<g class="rise" data-at="1600"><text x="0" y="162">Qwen3-4B (base)</text><rect x="170" y="149" width="176" height="20" fill="#7fa7d6"/><text x="352" y="164">0.490</text></g>
<g class="rise" data-at="2000"><text x="0" y="200">Gemini 3 Pro</text><rect x="170" y="187" width="239" height="20" fill="#7fa7d6"/><text x="415" y="202">0.665</text></g>
<g class="rise" data-at="2900"><text x="0" y="238" style="fill:#c9a227">EarlyModernNER</text><rect x="170" y="225" width="279" height="20" fill="#c9a227"/><text x="455" y="240" class="yr">0.775</text></g>
</svg>
```
[Strict F1 on a hand-annotated 100-page gold standard; 15 models tested, 6 shown.]{.jacob-method}
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.jacob-list}
EarlyModernNER vs Gemini 3 Pro:

- Slot error rate **0.331** vs 0.672
- **0** entities given the wrong type
- **26.7 s** per document vs 34.4 s
- **6.5 GB** peak GPU memory: runs locally, no API fee (Gemini: $8.88 per 100 documents)
:::
:::
:::

::: notes
3–4. Source: thesis chapter 2. Gold standard: 100 pages of olmOCR-2 output, hand-annotated for four types (toponym, person, commodity, organisation). Strict F1 counts boundary errors as misses.

How it was built: Qwen3-4B fine-tuned with LoRA, one specialist model per entity type run as a cascade, about 27,000 training entities reviewed by hand from a 25-million-token corpus, plus synthetic positive and negative examples. I tuned for precision over recall (strict precision 0.833), because a false entity creates a false historical pattern; a missed one only loses data.

Honest limit: recall is still lower than Gemini's (0.767 vs 0.816 partial recall).

Question for the room: would you choose precision or recall for your own extraction task?
:::

## A knowledge graph stores entities and typed relationships {#jacob-kg}

```{=html}
<div class="jacob-map"><span>1 Problem</span><span class="on">2 Graphs</span><span>3 Agents</span><span>4 Scale</span></div>
```

::: {.def}
[What is a knowledge graph?]{.def-term}
Entities are nodes; relationships are typed edges between them. Unlike a vector index, it can count, filter and join.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="flow">
  <div class="node"><b>Barbadoes · Barbedos · Barbadoss</b><span>spelling variants found by NER</span></div>
  <div class="arrow">→</div>
  <div class="node blue"><b>Barbados</b><span>one node, after disambiguation</span></div>
</div>
<div class="flow">
  <div class="node"><b>muscovado · brown sugar · molasses</b><span>variant products</span></div>
  <div class="arrow">→</div>
  <div class="node blue"><b>sugar</b><span>linked by IS_VARIANT_OF</span></div>
  <div class="arrow">→</div>
  <div class="node"><b>Customs records</b><span>43,000 rows of imports, 1696 to 1755</span></div>
</div>
```

::: {.stats}
::: {.stat}
[218,000]{.num}
[nodes]{.lbl}
:::
::: {.stat}
[692,000]{.num}
[edges]{.lbl}
:::
::: {.stat}
[1.74 million]{.num}
[text chunks linked to the entities they mention (rebuilt graph)]{.lbl}
:::
:::

::: notes
4–5. Source: thesis chapter 3. Entities were merged ("disambiguated") and linked with Qwen3.5-35B-A3B; the import-records spreadsheet was loaded into the same Neo4j graph so the graph can answer quantitative trade questions. The commodity hierarchy uses IS_VARIANT_OF and DERIVED_FROM edges.

The rebuilt graph (used by the best system later) links each entity to the exact chunk that mentions it, and chunks to sections and documents: 20,646 documents, 521,000 sections, 1.74 million chunks.

For a facility the same structure fits: sample, measured at, beamline; beamline, uses, technique; technique, reported in, paper.
:::

## GraphRAG: the graph decides which documents to read {#jacob-graphrag .motion}

```{=html}
<div class="jacob-map"><span>1 Problem</span><span class="on">2 Graphs</span><span>3 Agents</span><span>4 Scale</span></div>
```

::: {.def}
[What is GraphRAG?]{.def-term}
*Retrieval-augmented generation* (RAG) fetches text and gives it to a language model before it answers. **GraphRAG** uses a knowledge graph to choose which documents to fetch, then searches within them.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="flow">
  <div class="node rise" data-at="400"><b>Question</b></div>
  <div class="arrow rise" data-at="725">→</div>
  <div class="node blue rise" data-at="1050"><b>Seed entities</b><span>matched against 250,000 entity snippets</span></div>
  <div class="arrow rise" data-at="1375">→</div>
  <div class="node rise" data-at="1700"><b>Graph traversal</b><span>every document that mentions them</span></div>
  <div class="arrow rise" data-at="2025">→</div>
  <div class="node blue rise" data-at="2350"><b>Vector search</b><span>top 2 chunks per document</span></div>
  <div class="arrow rise" data-at="2675">→</div>
  <div class="node rise" data-at="3000"><b>Language model</b><span>answers from the top 20 chunks</span></div>
</div>
<p class="motion-caption rise" data-at="3800" style="font-size:0.65em;color:#f3ead3">Better documents than plain RAG. But the model still only sees fragments.</p>
```

::: notes
5–6. This is the "True GraphRAG" system from chapter 3. Seed entities come from a separate index of 250,000 short entity-relationship snippets embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-8B. The graph finds every document mentioning those entities; vector search then picks the two most similar chunks per document; the top 20 go to the model.

Microsoft Research's 2024 GraphRAG is a different variant (it summarises graph communities); I tested graph-directed retrieval because it keeps answers tied to documents.

The caption sets up the next two slides.
:::

[Method: 30 questions in 5 difficulty tiers; I graded each answer on 5 criteria, up to 5 points each. Questions 1–17 were not strictly blind (a labelling bug kept each system on the same letter); Improved Scratchpad was scored on 23 questions. One grader, one corpus: read as a pilot, not a benchmark.]{.jacob-method}

::: notes
6–7. Source: thesis chapter 3, Evaluation. Criteria: groundedness, completeness, accuracy, synthesis, usefulness. Local model throughout: Qwen3.5-27B with an 8,192-token context.

Two results to say out loud. First, in red: adding knowledge-graph facts to plain RAG made it worse, because vector search still chose the documents and the graph facts compounded its mistakes. Second: every graph-directed variant plateaued near 15.7.

Be upfront about the method limits on the slide; this audience will ask. The grading bug and the 23-question subset are both in the thesis.
:::

## Why graph-directed retrieval plateaued near 15.7 {#jacob-plateau}

```{=html}
<div class="jacob-map"><span>1 Problem</span><span class="on">2 Graphs</span><span>3 Agents</span><span>4 Scale</span></div>
```

::: {.cards}
::: {.card .warn}
[Extraction errors]{.kicker}

#### Noisy graph

Incomplete merging of entities by the language model left duplicates and false links.
:::
::: {.card .warn}
[Coarse edges]{.kicker}

#### Document, not passage

The graph knew which document mentioned an entity, not where in it.
:::
::: {.card .warn}
[Fragments]{.kicker}

#### Never a whole document

The model read 20 chunks, without the text around them.
:::
::: {.card .warn}
[Synthesis]{.kicker}

#### Misread evidence

Answers blended contradictory sources and hallucinated material.
:::
:::

> Better retrieval did not fix **how the model read the evidence**.

::: notes
7–8. Source: thesis chapter 3, "Graph Directed Retrieval" and "Self-Correction". Self-RAG (grading passages and rewriting queries) helped plain RAG most (+3 points) but added only 0.06 over the best graph variant: it could not supply evidence retrieval had missed.

Also worth one sentence: graph construction is expensive in general. Microsoft Research reports its original GraphRAG indexing at roughly 1,000 times the cost of a vector index (LazyGraphRAG blog post, 2024).

This sets up part 3: the fix was to change how the system reads.
:::

## What worked: an agent that takes notes on each source {#jacob-scratchpad .motion}

```{=html}
<div class="jacob-map"><span>1 Problem</span><span>2 Graphs</span><span class="on">3 Agents</span><span>4 Scale</span></div>
```

::: {.def}
[What is an agent?]{.def-term}
A language model that calls tools (search, a file reader, a database) and decides its next step from what it finds.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="flow">
  <div class="node rise" data-at="400"><b>Split the question</b><span>into sub-questions</span></div>
  <div class="arrow rise" data-at="700">→</div>
  <div class="node blue rise" data-at="1000"><b>Retrieve 35 diverse chunks</b><span>penalise near-duplicates</span></div>
  <div class="arrow rise" data-at="1300">→</div>
  <div class="node rise" data-at="1600"><b>Read the neighbours</b><span>"turn the page"</span></div>
  <div class="arrow rise" data-at="1900">→</div>
  <div class="node blue rise" data-at="2200"><b>One note per source</b><span>facts, quotes, relevance</span></div>
</div>
<div class="flow">
  <div class="node rise" data-at="2600"><b>Query the graph</b><span>agent writes a database query when numbers are needed</span></div>
  <div class="arrow rise" data-at="2900">→</div>
  <div class="node blue rise" data-at="3200"><b>Flag conflicts</b><span>between sources</span></div>
  <div class="arrow rise" data-at="3500">→</div>
  <div class="node rise" data-at="3800"><b>Answer</b><span>from the notes, in date order</span></div>
  <div class="arrow rise" data-at="4100">→</div>
  <div class="node after rise" data-at="4400"><b>Verify</b><span>flags claims with no note behind them</span></div>
</div>
```

::: {.stats}
::: {.stat}
[17.90 / 25]{.num}
[mean score; next best 16.06]{.lbl}
:::
::: {.stat}
[63 of 70]{.num}
[head-to-head wins]{.lbl}
:::
::: {.stat}
[~10 vs 4.2]{.num}
[unique documents per question vs other systems]{.lbl}
:::
::: {.stat}
[593 s]{.num}
[per question, 22.9 model calls: the cost]{.lbl}
:::
:::

::: notes
8–9. Source: thesis chapter 3, "Historical Processing" and "Evaluation". This is the Improved Scratchpad. The diversity step is a determinantal point process, which penalises redundant chunks. "Turn the page" expands each chunk to its neighbours. The agent decides whether the graph is needed and writes a Neo4j Cypher query itself.

The design came from asking how a historian reads: take notes on each source separately, compare them, look for disagreements, then write. Standard iterative refinement failed here: after 35 rewrites the draft drifted and every answer hallucinated.

The cost is real: about 7 times slower than the next system. For a research tool, a 10-minute answer that surfaces 10 sources is still faster than reading one.
:::

## The larger model asked the graph a narrower question {#jacob-cypher .motion}

```{=html}
<div class="jacob-map"><span>1 Problem</span><span>2 Graphs</span><span class="on">3 Agents</span><span>4 Scale</span></div>
```

> How much ginger did the British Caribbean colonies export between 1696 and 1755, and how did volumes change over time?

```{=html}
<div class="motion-card bad rise" data-at="900"><b>Claude Opus 4.7</b> (frontier model, via API)<br>Wrote a more restrictive database query. Got back 1697 to 1714 only, and reported that the record stops there. <span class="verdict-bad">Incorrect: the graph holds 1696 to 1755.</span></div>
<div class="motion-card good rise" data-at="2600"><b>Qwen3.6-35B-A3B</b> (open model, run locally)<br>Retrieved the full record: a peak of 1,639 tons in 1735, then a fall of over 90% to 79.9 tons in 1744. <span class="verdict-good">Correct, and checked against the graph.</span></div>
<p class="motion-caption rise" data-at="4000" style="font-size:0.65em;color:#f3ead3">Retrieval and synthesis are separate steps, so we could see exactly which step failed.</p>
```

::: notes
9–10. Source: thesis chapter 3, case study (question 1), and the model-swap test at the end of it. Same pipeline, only the language model changed.

This is the slide for scientists: a controlled comparison with one variable. The larger, more expensive model was not better here; it wrote a narrower WHERE clause and so had less evidence. Both models were careful about the evidence they had. The architecture made the failure diagnosable instead of "the AI got it wrong".

The same graph-query step is what answered the sugar question from slide 1: Jamaica first overtook Barbados in 1719, 5,087 tons to 4,369. Improved Scratchpad was the one system of eight that got it.
:::

## For thousands of documents, well-organised text is enough {#jacob-semistructured}

```{=html}
<div class="jacob-map"><span>1 Problem</span><span>2 Graphs</span><span class="on">3 Agents</span><span>4 Scale</span></div>
```

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
What an agent needs:

- Folders with meaningful names
- Plain text or Markdown with consistent headings
- A few lines of metadata at the top of each file: date, author, instrument
- Filenames a person could guess
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.def}
[What is semi-structured text?]{.def-term}
Ordinary documents with a predictable shape: headings, labelled fields, consistent names. Not a database.
:::

Examples: a facility's manuals, procedures and logbooks.
:::
:::

> No index, no graph: the agent searches, opens files and reads around what it finds. **Good documentation practice is now good practice for AI search.**

::: notes
10–11. The lesson from my best system generalises: what helped was reading around a hit and taking notes, not a more elaborate index. Current agents do exactly that with plain text tools.

Evidence from software: Boris Cherny, who leads Claude Code at Anthropic, has said early versions used a local vector database, and that agentic search with plain text tools worked better and was simpler.

For collections in the thousands, organised text plus an agent is often enough. It rewards habits that already help people: clear names, consistent structure, dates.

Question for the room: what format is your beamline documentation in now?
:::

## MCP and Linked Open Data connect an agent to data that already exists {#jacob-mcp}

```{=html}
<div class="jacob-map"><span>1 Problem</span><span>2 Graphs</span><span class="on">3 Agents</span><span>4 Scale</span></div>
```

::: {.defs}
::: {.def}
[What is MCP?]{.def-term}
The *Model Context Protocol*: an open standard for connecting a language model to tools and data. A connector written once works with any assistant that supports it. Released by Anthropic in late 2024; governed by the Linux Foundation since December 2025.
:::
::: {.def}
[What is Linked Open Data?]{.def-term}
Open data in which every person, place, institution or paper has a **persistent identifier**. Datasets that share identifiers can be joined, even if they were built separately (Wikidata, OpenAlex, ORCID, ROR, DOIs).
:::
:::

```{=html}
<div class="flow">
  <div class="node"><b>Your files</b></div>
  <div class="node"><b>A document archive</b></div>
  <div class="node blue"><b>OpenAlex</b><span>research papers</span></div>
  <div class="node blue"><b>Wikidata</b><span>people, places, things</span></div>
  <div class="node blue"><b>A knowledge graph</b><span>one tool among several</span></div>
</div>
<div class="loopback">↕ one agent reaches all of these through MCP</div>
```

[The Canadian Light Source is ROR **001bvc968** and OpenAlex **I83308685**: any dataset using those identifiers joins to its 3,169 works.]{.jacob-method}

::: notes
11–12. Identifiers checked through the OpenAlex API on 13 November 2026.

Before MCP, every link between a model and a data source was custom code. Now there are standard connectors, including ready-made ones for OpenAlex and Wikidata. The knowledge graph becomes one tool the agent calls when a question is about relationships.

Link back to slide 6: in my corpus a language model had to decide that "Barbadoes" and "Barbados" are the same place. Shared identifiers turn that guess into a lookup.
:::

## Which approach fits which collection size {#jacob-scale}

```{=html}
<div class="jacob-map"><span>1 Problem</span><span>2 Graphs</span><span>3 Agents</span><span class="on">4 Scale</span></div>
```

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[Hundreds to thousands of documents]{.kicker}

#### Agentic search

Over well-organised text. No index.

[A facility's manuals and logbooks]{.fact}
:::
::: {.card .accent}
[Hundreds of thousands to millions]{.kicker}

#### An index the agent calls

Graph and vector indexes, reached as tools. Worth the build cost here.

[My 1.74 million chunks]{.fact}
:::
::: {.card}
[Hundreds of millions]{.kicker}

#### Linked Open Data

Connect to what exists through MCP. Do not rebuild it.

[The literature: ~315 million works]{.fact}
:::
:::

> The software finds and ranks. **People read and judge.**

::: notes
14–15. Summary. For thousands of documents, agentic search over organised text is often enough. At millions, an agent cannot read everything per query, so you need an index; that is where graphs and vectors are worth their cost, as tools the agent calls. At the scale of the literature, connect to open infrastructure.

Across all of it, the job is discovery: finding and ranking what a person should read. My best system was the one designed around how a historian reads, and it still ends with a person checking the sources.

Hand back to Jim.
:::
